title: Sawan Fasting? This No-Onion, No-Garlic Paneer Sabji Is Ready in 20 Minutes
excerpt: A rich, creamy paneer curry that follows sattvic cooking principles for Shravan fasting — using whole spices, tomatoes, and cashew paste instead of the usual onion-garlic base.
body:
• This vrat-friendly paneer sabji skips onion and garlic entirely, relying on whole spices, tomatoes, and cashew paste to build a rich, creamy gravy in about 20 minutes.
  • The recipe follows sattvic cooking principles observed during Sawan (Shravan), the Hindu holy month that falls in July-August when many devotees fast on Mondays.
  • Key ingredients — paneer, tomatoes, ginger, green chillies, ghee, and whole spices like bay leaf, cinnamon, and cardamom — are readily available at most grocery stores.
  • The dish pairs well with puri, kuttu ki roti, or plain rice for a complete fasting meal.

Sawan, or Shravan, is well underway — and for millions of Hindus observing Monday fasts this month, the daily question is the same: what to cook that is both sattvic and satisfying. This no-onion, no-garlic paneer sabji answers that question with minimal effort and maximum flavor.

Why No Onion and No Garlic?

In the Hindu tradition, Sawan is considered one of the holiest months, dedicated to Lord Shiva. Many devotees observe partial or complete fasts, particularly on Mondays (Sawan Somvar). Sattvic cooking — which avoids onion, garlic, and other "rajasic" and "tamasic" foods believed to stimulate restlessness or lethargy — is the default during these fasting periods.

For cooks accustomed to building flavor through an onion-garlic base, this restriction can feel limiting. The trick is leaning harder on other aromatics: whole spices, ginger, green chillies, and hing (asafoetida) do the heavy lifting instead.

"Sattvic cooking — which avoids onion, garlic, and other "rajasic" and "tamasic" foods believed to stimulate restlessness or lethargy — is the default during these fasting periods."

The Recipe

This version draws from recipes published by KuchPakRahaHai and Cookpad, adapted for a straightforward weeknight cook.

Ingredients: 200g paneer (cubed), 3 medium tomatoes (pureed), 1-inch ginger (grated), 2 green chillies (slit), 2 tablespoons ghee, 2 tablespoons cream or malai, 1 tablespoon cashew paste or melon seed (magaj) paste, 1 teaspoon sugar, and whole spices — 1 bay leaf, 1 small cinnamon stick, 3 green cardamom pods, a pinch of hing, 1 teaspoon cumin seeds, plus red chilli powder, turmeric, coriander powder, garam masala, and kasuri methi to taste.

Method: Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan. Add the bay leaf, cinnamon, cardamom, and cumin seeds; let them splutter for 30 seconds. Add hing, ginger, and green chillies. Sauté briefly, then pour in the tomato puree. Cook on medium heat for 8-10 minutes until the oil separates and the raw tomato smell disappears.

Stir in the cashew paste, sugar, and dry spice powders. Add half a cup of water if the gravy is too thick. Slide in the paneer cubes and simmer for 3-4 minutes. Finish with cream, a sprinkle of garam masala, and crushed kasuri methi. Serve hot.

Tips for a Better Result

The cashew paste is what gives the gravy its body without onions. Soak 8-10 cashews in warm water for 15 minutes and blend to a smooth paste. Melon seeds (magaj) are a traditional alternative — they produce a slightly lighter, nuttier gravy. Either works.

Do not skip the sugar. A teaspoon counterbalances the tomato's acidity and rounds out the gravy in a way that salt alone cannot. And use full-fat cream or malai rather than milk — the richness is the point.

For paneer, fresh blocks from an Indian grocery store are ideal, but even supermarket paneer works if you soak the cubes in warm salted water for 10 minutes before adding them. This softens them and prevents the rubbery texture that plagues overcooked paneer.

Serving Suggestions

Pair the sabji with puri for a classic fasting plate. Kuttu ki roti (buckwheat flatbread) or sama ke chawal (barnyard millet rice) are other traditional vrat accompaniments. For a simpler option, plain steamed rice works well — the creamy gravy carries the meal on its own.

The recipe scales easily for families and keeps well in the refrigerator for a day or two — useful when you are fasting every Monday through the month and want to cook once rather than four times.
